list.listitem: Hypokalemic periodic paralysis (HPP) is characterized by episodic reversible attacks of muscle weakness associated with decreased serum potassium levels. It occurs in familial and thyrotoxic forms.C
The McManis short exercise test can be useful in identifying patients with HPP between attacks.B

Acute treatment of HPP involves potassium administration, which can shorten duration of paralytic episode. Patients should be monitored closely for rebound hyperkalemia, as it can occur in at least 40% of patients.B
Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce episodes of familial HPP, and treatment of thyrotoxicosis prevents thyrotoxic HPP in susceptible patients.A

background.definition: HPP is a muscle disorder with reversible attacks of muscle weakness caused by decreased serum potassium levels. It occurs in a familial form and a thyrotoxic form.

list.listitem: The exact frequency of familial HPP is not known; the prevalence has been estimated at 1:100,000 in Danish registries.
The exact frequency of thyrotoxic HPP is not known, but it appears to be most common in Asian thyrotoxic populations.
Approximately 2% of patients with thyrotoxicosis in China and Japan have associated HPP.
Familial HPP is an autosomally dominantly inherited condition caused by mutations in the genes encoding skeletal muscle ion channels. Variable phenotypes exist in families.
Thyrotoxic HPP is due to thyroid hormone-stimulated increase in Na/K ATPase activity.
Risk factors for thyrotoxic HPP include male sex (20:1 male to female ratio) and Asian descent.

Eighty percent of cases of familial HPP are due to point mutations in the voltage-gated calcium channel gene on chromosome 1. Other cases have been attributed to mutations in the voltage-gated sodium channel on chromosome 17. The mutated ion channels cause periodic influx into skeletal muscle cells, resulting in hypokalemia and an inability of the muscles to contract.

Thyrotoxic HPP is thought to be due to thyroid hormone stimulation of Na/K ATPase activity, which causes an intracellular shift of potassium, hypokalemia, and paralysis. Thyrotoxic patients who manifest HPP may have a genetic predisposition to Na/K-ATPase activation, which could account for ethnic difference in incidence.
HPP is characterized by episodic reversible attacks of muscle weakness associated with decreased serum potassium levels.C
Familial HPP usually requires a pattern of attacks in order to confirm diagnosis. See .C
The McManis short exercise test can be useful in identifying patients with HPP between attacks.B
Permanent myopathy, in which weakness persists between attacks, can be seen in older adults with familial HPP. This can be confirmed by muscle biopsy, which reveals vacuolar degeneration.B

Differential.Differential_Features: Hypokalemia occurs during and between attacks; can occur in the setting of renal or GI potassium loss
Persistent rather than episodic muscle weakness, associated with atrophy

Differential.Differential_Name: Other neurological/muscular disease causing flaccid paralysis
Differential.Differential_Features: Not clearly associated with hypokalemia and not improving once potassium normalizes
Autosomally inherited condition of sodium channels that leads to periodic paralysis associated with hyperkalemia

list.listitem: HPP usually presents as attacks of symmetrical painless limb muscle weakness with decreased deep tendon reflexes, sparing respiratory and bulbar muscles, associated with hypokalemia (K <3.5). Paralysis spontaneously resolves after several hours or as potassium normalizes. Triggers include strenuous exercise several hours prior to attack, a prior meal rich in carbohydrates, alcohol use, or use of medications such as β-mimetics, insulin, or corticosteroids.
Familial HPP usually requires a pattern of attacks in order to confirm diagnosis ().

Thyrotoxic HPP, which can be seen with any cause of thyrotoxicosis, may be accompanied by signs/symptoms of thyrotoxicosis (lid lag, goiter, tachycardia, weight loss, diarrhea, tremor), but nearly half of patients have no obvious symptoms related to hyperthyroidism.
Diagnosis of HPP is usually based on clinical examination, the presence of family history of the disease, changes in serum potassium during attacks, and the response to treatment.

During a paralytic attack, electromyography reveals low-amplitude compound muscle action potential of the tested muscles and muscular inexcitability in response to direct electrical stimulation that disappears during remission.

During the period between attacks, exercise can induce weakness in patients with HPP. This can be demonstrated in the McManis short exercise test, an electrophysiological test in which compound muscle action potential is measured during and after 2 to 5 minutes of intermittent strong voluntary muscle contraction.
Glucose/insulin challenge can provoke attacks of paralysis, but should only be done in a carefully monitored setting, given risk of cardiac arrhythmias.

Familial HPP can progress to permanent myopathy, with weakness persisting between acute attacks, a diagnosis that is confirmed by vacuoles seen on muscle biopsy, which are the result of proliferation and degeneration of membranous organelles.
Thyroid function tests (low thyroid-stimulating hormone, high free thyroid hormone levels) distinguish familial from thyrotoxic HPP.
Gene testing can be used in suspected familial HPP, but is expensive and most useful when screening family members of patients with a known ion channel mutation.
Suspect HPP in patients with symmetrical, painless limb muscle weakness associated with hypokalemia. Diagnosis is primarily clinical.
The McManis short exercise test can confirm the diagnosis.
Order thyroid function tests and take a careful family history to distinguish thyrotoxic from familial HPP.
Diagnostic criteria for familial HPP are shown in .
Acute treatment of HPP involves potassium administration, which can shorten duration of paralytic episode. Patients should be monitored closely for rebound hyperkalemia.B
Preventative treatment in familial HPP includes carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, which reduce frequency and severity of paralytic episodes.A
Treatment of thyrotoxic HPP includes propranolol and definitive treatment of thyrotoxicosis.B
Mild exercise and avoidance of carbohydrate-rich meals may help prevent recurrent paralytic attacks.C
Acute treatment of HPP involves potassium administration, which can shorten the duration of the paralysis and prevent life-threatening hypokalemic-related arrhythmias.

The dosing of potassium is controversial and not standardized; some experts recommend KCl 10 mEq/h or 2 g (20-30 mEq) every 2 hours. Serum potassium levels should be carefully monitored every 2 to 4 hours during replacement. Morbidity and mortality in patients with periodic paralysis are related to hypokalemic complications such as ventricular arrhythmias. Therefore, patients should be monitored electrocardiographically during treatment.

Total body potassium stores are normal in patients with HPP. Potassium is released from cells rapidly when paralysis subsides, leading to rebound hyperkalemia in at least 40% of patients particularly if they received more than 90 mEq of KCl within 24 hours. Lower doses of KCl (total dose 50 mEq or less) may be efficacious while substantially reducing the risk of hyperkalemia.

Nonselective β-blockers such as propranolol may reduce the contribution of hyperadrenergic activity in thyrotoxic HPP, but only case reports are available. They also may prevent recurrent attacks of thyrotoxic HPP.

Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors, such as acetazolamide or dichlorphenamide (not available in US) reduce future episodes in familial HPP. The mechanism of action is unknown, but they may act on potassium channels implicated in regulating muscle excitability. Dichlorphenamide may have a small impact on attack rate.

Studies have shown that carbonic anhydrase inhibitors decrease the mean attack rate approximately 1 attack per week, decrease attack severity and increase muscle strength by 10% compared to placebo. Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors can precipitate recurrent attacks of thyrotoxic HPP and should not be used for treatment of thyrotoxic HPP.
In thyrotoxic HPP, definitive therapy of thyrotoxicosis, via antithyroid drugs, radioactive iodine, or thyroidectomy, is essential to prevent recurrence of paralytic episodes.

Lifestyle modifications, such as regular mild (ie, not strenuous) exercise and avoidance of carbohydrate-rich meals may help prevent recurrent paralytic attacks, although this has not been proven in controlled studies.
Patients with thyrotoxic HPP should be referred to an endocrinologist for management of thyrotoxicosis.
Consider neurology referral for patients with familial HPP.

Precautions should be taken during anesthetic procedures in HPP patients, including avoiding IV glucose and monitoring temperature carefully, given potential risk of malignant hyperthermia and exacerbation of paralysis.
Episodes of paralysis in familial HPP usually begin in the second decade and are highest in frequency from second to fourth decades of life, after which frequency declines.C
Familial HPP may progress to a myopathy, with persistent muscle weakness between acute attacks; some propose it affects all patients older than 50 years to some degree.C
Once thyrotoxicosis is definitively treated, thyrotoxic HPP episodes will not recur.A

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Familial Hypokalemic Periodic Paralysis.
feature.feature_body: Two or more attacks of muscle weakness with documented serum K <3.5 mEq/L. One attack of muscle weakness in the proband and one attack of weakness in one relative with documented serum K <3.5 mEq/L in at least one attack. Three of 6 clinical or laboratory features as outlined below: Onset in the first or second decade. Attack duration (muscle weakness involving 1 or more limbs) >2 h. Positive triggers (high carbohydrate-rich meal, rest after exercise, stress). Improvement with potassium intake. Positive family history of genetically confirmed skeletal calcium or sodium channel mutation. Positive McManis short exercise test. Exclusion of other causes of hypokalemia (renal, adrenal, thyroid dysfunction, renal tubular acidosis, diuretic, and laxative abuse). From Sansone V, Meola G, Links TP, Panzeri M, Rose MR. Treatment for periodic paralysis (Cochrane Review). The Cochrane Library 2008 Issue 2. Chichester, UK: John Wiley & Sons, Ltd.
